The long term forecast period continues to be defined by an 
amplified mid/upper-level synoptic weather pattern. The antecedent 
ridging over the west-central CONUS is progged to strengthen this 
weekend, with 500mb heights over the Great Plains states rising 
towards the 99th percentile of LREF model climatology on Saturday 
and Sunday. At the same time, troughing will dig deeper into the 
Eastern Seaboard, with heights off the Carolina coast plummeting 
down below the 10th percentile early next week. Eastern Kentucky 
will be positioned in between these two anomalously strong features 
for the rest of the period, and guidance collectively resolves a 
prolonged regime of northwesterly flow aloft as a result. A series 
of shortwave disturbances is progged to navigate through this flow 
and approach the forecast area over the course of the next week. As 
they arrive, they will interact with increasing temperatures and 
greater low-level moisture to produce periodic shower/storm chances. 
Confidence in specific timing/intensity details decreases with time 
though.  

Forecast confidence is at its highest this weekend, during the 
pattern's transition period. As the influence of the midlevel 
ridging to our west grows on Friday, the surface high pressure 
system responsible for today and tomorrow's pleasant will shift east 
for Saturday. This allows low-level flow to adopt a more west-
southwesterly orientation and gradually return moisture to the 
atmospheric column from SW to NE. Generic rain shower chances 
accordingly re-enter the forecast in the southern half of the 
forecast area after midnight on Saturday morning, when the first 
shortwave impulse is expected to arrive aloft. This initial round of 
activity is not expected to pose a risk for hazardous weather, but 
the related cloud cover should keep Saturday morning's MinTs 
insulated within the mid/upper 60s. It may also prevent the area's 
conventional overnight ridge-valley temperature splits from coming 
to fruition. Filtered diurnal warming and continued low-level WAA 
yields high temperatures in the low/mid 80s on Saturday afternoon, 
when relatively deeper moisture will begin spreading across the CWA. 
LREF mean PWATs rise to between 1.5 inches in the Big Sandy region 
and 1.8 inches closer to Lake Cumberland on Saturday evening, and 
the arrival of the next impulse aloft should spark more meaningful 
showers and storms by then. Saturday's PM activity is more likely to 
come in the form of thunderstorms than anything that develops on 
Friday night/Saturday morning, but that convection is still not 
expected to be severe. While it may still produce frequent lightning 
and heavy rainfall, it is generally expected to wind down overnight 
with the loss of diurnal heating. If there is enough clearing in its 
wake, the area's conventional ridge/valley temperature splits could 
materialize by Sunday morning. Likewise, and especially if grounds 
are wet across the area, nighttime radiation fog is plausible.   

The pattern continues to amplify headed into next week, and the 
growing influence of the ridging to our west should allow 
temperatures to warm into the upper 80s on Sunday and then towards 
the lower 90s on Monday and Tuesday. This corresponds with a return 
to seasonably appropriate dewpoints in the upper 60s/lower 70s, and 
together, this establishes a favorable thermodynamic environment for 
relatively stronger thunderstorms next week. Additional disturbances 
working their way around the ridge via the persistent NW flow will 
provide the dynamic forcing necessary for storm initiation, but 
there is considerable forecast uncertainty surrounding the arrival 
time of each wave. Pattern recognition suggests that some of this 
convective activity could take the form of more organized ridge-
riding MCSes, but the intensity of that activity would be highly 
sensitive to both the evolution of upstream activity and its 
relation to the diurnal instability cycle. The currently-available 
deterministic model data lacks the resolution to resolve these finer-
scale convective details, but there are some useful signals showing 
up in ensemble, analog, and AI/ML guidance. 

Various machine learning outlook models continue to paint severe 
hazard probability contours across our CWA early next week. There is 
noticeably less of a signal with the experimental output for 
Sunday's setup, but recent guidance suggests that there may be a 
consensus time frame emerging between Monday night and Tuesday
